title: CHAN v HAMILTON CITY COUNCIL
text:
IN THE EMPLOYMENT RELATIONS AUTHORITY
AUCKLAND
I TE RATONGA AHUMANA TAIMAHI
TĀMAKI MAKAURAU ROHE
[2025] NZERA 524
3202539
BETWEEN GENEVA CHAN
Applicant
AND HAMILTON CITY COUNCIL
R espondent
Member of Authority: Eleanor Robinson
Representatives: Allan Halse, advocate for the Applicant
Tom Jarman, counsel for the Respondent
Investigation Meeting: 26 to 28 May 2026 in Hamilton
Submissions and/or further 12 June and 13 July 2026 from the Applicant
evidence 25 June 2026 from the Respondent
Determination: 4 August 2026
DETERMINATION OF THE AUTHORITY
Employment Relationship Problem
[1] The Applicant, Geneva Chan, claims that she was unjustifiably dismissed and
unjustifiably disadvantaged by the Respondent, Hamilton City Council (HCC).
[2] Ms Chan further claims that she was unjustifiably disadvantaged by the way in which
HCC handled her complaint of bullying.
[3] HCC denies that Ms Chan was unjustifiably dismissed or unjustifiably disadvantaged,
and claims that it acted appropriately.
The Authority’s investigation
[4] The Authority received written and, under oath or affirmation, oral evidence from the
Applicant witnesses: Geneva Chan, Brittany Chan, Colin Chan, Anna Chan, Ashleigh Sanders,
Ben Wynne-Jones, Corrine Ellis, Lisa O’Hara, Tarrant Peterson, and Ashleigh Morgan-Fish.
[5] The Authority received written and, under oath or affirmation, oral evidence from the
Respondent witnesses: Natasha Clark, Catherine Nichols, Cheridan Mathers, Grant Kother and
Alejandro Calero.

[6] Oral and written submissions were received from Mr Halse for the Applicant and from
Mr Jarman for the Respondent. Whilst I have not referred to all the submissions made by the
parties; I have fully considered them.
[7] As permitted by s 174E of the Employment Relations Act 2000 (the Act) this
determination has stated findings of fact and law, expressed conclusions on issues necessary to
dispose of the matter and specified orders made. It has not recorded all evidence and
submissions received.
Issues
[8] The issues requiring investigation are whether or not Ms Chan was
• Unjustifiably dismissed by HCC?
• Unjustifiably disadvantaged by the way in which HCC handled her bullying
complaint?
Background
[9] Hamilton Zoo is an accredited member of the Zoological and Aquarium Association
for Australasia (ZAA), and reports to the World Association of Zoos and Aquariums. ZAA has
species programmes by region and all species native and endemic to New Zealand must be held
with authority to hold absolutely protected wildlife which is issued by the Department of
Conservation.
[10] To gain accreditation to ZAA Hamilton Zoo has an onsite audit every three years.
Between the three yearly audits Hamilton Zoo has to maintain standards by working with the
programme guidelines and instructions. In addition to the ZAA audits, the Zoo is audited
annually by the Ministry of Primary Industries.
[11] Ms Chan commenced employment with HCC as a Zookeeper (Birds and Ectothermals)
working at Hamilton Zoo (the Zoo) on 18 March 2019. Initially this was a one year position to
cover maternity leave but it became a permanent role in March 2020.
[12] Ms Chan worked as part of a team of seven with varying levels of experience. Ms Chan
reported to Grant Kother, Team Leader of Birds and Ectotherms (BAE) until he was temporarily
seconded to another area of the Zoo in 2020, when she reported to Ms Mathers for that period.
[13] Ms Chan was provided with an individual employment agreement which stated at
clause 7.2 that she would “comply with the Council’s policies and rules always”. Ms Chan

confirmed that she had read and understood the terms and conditions, and she had signed the
Employment Agreement, initialling each page.
[14] Ms Chan said she initially had a good working relationship with Mr Kother and with
Ms Mathers and enjoyed working with the BAE team.
Bullying
[15] Ms Chan said she had started to experience bullying behaviour towards her by her
manager. She said there had been unhappiness in the BAE team. She referred to the BAE team
members not being allowed to express their opinions and to people feeling upset.
[16] Ms Chan said she shared a house with Mr Calero and that she dated the change from
when he became Second in Charge (2IC) in the BAE team. She felt Mr Calero reported things
she had been speaking about at home to management.
[17] Mr Calero denied that he had reported what Ms Chan had been saying to him, although
he did speak to members of the management team as part of his role.
[18] Other employees and former employees of the BAE team were questioned about the
issue of bullying in the BAE team:
Ms Morgan-Fish said there was not a good culture in the BAE team, however she had
not spoken to anyone in the management team about her view;
Mr Wynne-Jones said Ms Chan had not felt she was treated fairly;
Ms Saunders had worked for a short time with Ms Chan, she had raised a personal
grievance in connection with a former Zoo management member, however that related
to events prior to Ms Chan’s period with the BAE team; and
Mr Peterson said he had worked with Ms Chan on the BAE team for a period of two
years. He said he felt confident about approaching management members if he had
concerns, and that they would listen if he felt he could not speak to other managers,
[19] Mr Kother said Ms Chan had told him she found him ‘intimidating’ but he was unaware
that she considered she had been bullied by him, and he had not been advised of this by her or
anyone else.
[20] Ms Mathers said that Ms Chan had not raised any concerns about bullying with her,
although Ms Chan had sometimes discussed with her concerns she had about her colleagues.

[21] Ms Clark had been the HR Business Partner during Mr Chan’s employment. The BAE
team was within her portfolio. Ms Clark explained that the HCC Bullying and Harassment
Policy set out the procedure for addressing bullying concerns.
[22] An employee could raise his or her concerns with any member of the Zoo management
team if they felt unable to raise it at a higher level within their team or if it concerned his or her
direct manager.
[23] Ms Clark said Ms Chan had not raised any concerns about bullying by Mr Kother or
Ms Mathers with her. Nor to her knowledge had she done so to any other Zoo management
member.
[24] Ms Chan said the bullying behaviour had only happened a few months before her
employment ended. She had did not take her concerns to any management members outside of
the BAE team, nor did she follow any of the options set out in the HCC Bullying and
Harassment Policy because she did not want to adversely affect her career. noting that her
position at the Zoo was her first permanent role.
[25] Prior to March 2021 there were some incidents relating to Ms Chan in her employment
at the Zoo.
January 2020
[26] On 31 January 2020 a Hochstetter’s frog was discovered with its leg squashed under a
rock. The frog was alive and removed from the enclosure for isolation and veterinary care, but
died a few days later. Ms Chan was the last person to check the frogs four days earlier.
[27] Ms Mathers had been acting Team Leader BAE at the time because Mr Kother was on
secondment. She said she had spoken to Ms Chan following the death of the frog and shown
her how to check and safely position the frogs.
[28] No disciplinary action was taken following the incident.
May 2020t
[29] In May 2020 Ms Chan stepped on a Princess Parrot which was behind her in an
enclosure, the parrot suffered multiple fractures and had to be euthanised.
[30] Ms Chan said the parrot was very friendly and was often around the keepers’ feet. At
the time she had been rushing to attend a team meeting and turned and accidently stood on the
parrot. She had been distressed at the incident.

[31] The death was considered to be an accident and Mr Kother said he had made it clear
to Ms Chan that she had not been at fault in the incident.
February 2021
[32] Ms Chan said that she was reprimanded for an incident involving Ms Morgan-Fish in
February 2021. She said that Ms Morgan-Fish had left after a meeting regarding a non-work
injury held with Mr Kother, Ms Mathers and Ms Clark.
[33] Ms Morgan-Fish said she had suffered a severe hand injury which had impacted on the
use of her hand. During her recovery period there were weekly meetings with the BAE
management team to plan her work activities.
[34] Following one such meeting in February 2021 Ms Chan said Ms Morgan-Fish appeared
to be upset, so she asked her if she would like to accompany her to assist with looking for
reptiles. During their time together Ms Morgan-Fish had discussed with her how upsetting she
had found the meeting.
[35] Mr Kother said during the meeting with Ms Morgan-Fish she had become upset and he
had told her she could go home. However she had wanted to stay at the Zoo so he instructed
her to work with Mr Calero. After the meeting he had gone to find her and radioed when he
was unable to do so, finding her with Ms Chan He had asked Ms Morgan-Fish to return to
work with Mr Calero.
[36] After Ms Morgan-Fish had left, Ms Chan said Mr Kother came to find her and asked
why she had been with Ms Morgan-Fish and if they had discussed the meeting. Ms Chan denied
they had talked about the meeting.
[37] Afterwards Ms Chan said she felt guilty about having lied to Mr Kother and went to
tell him the truth. She said Mr Kother told her that she should have acted more appropriately
by telling him that she and Ms Morgan-Fish needed a break and were going off-site. She said
she understood her actions had been wrong and apologised.
[38] Mr Kother confirmed that when he spoke to Ms Chan she told him that the meeting had
not been discussed but later she had sought him out and confessed that she had not told him the
truth. He had not taken any action because he considered it to be an isolated incident.
March 2021: Guinea fowl chick incident
[39] Mr Kother said that a team member of BAE raised the idea of hand rearing birds and
suggested bringing in some chicken eggs to artificially incubate and gain experience in the
development and rearing of birds. He said the Zoo is involved in captive breeding of endangered

native species, so it was considered an important skill for the BAE team to have and considered
to be a training opportunity with a non-endangered exotic bird species.
[40] Mr Kother said he suggested that rather than chicken eggs, the eggs of Guinea Fowl
birds were incubated and reared. Mr Kother said the Guinea Fowl were free ranging around
the Zoo and there were fertile eggs available for incubation purposes. It was a voluntary project,
and he sent an email on 3 March 2021 setting out what would be involved:
- You will be paired up into teams (to be decided by you) to help cover RDOs. …
- Each pair will be given 3 eggs …
- Each pair will be given an incubator for which you will be responsible for
maintaining.
- Cheridan and I will not be directly involved in the process, so you will be required
to research and decide which eggs to select, incubation parameters, development
checks, servicing your incubator, information sheets, etc.
- Once hatched the birds … will be reared together at the zoo. You will then decide
as a team, diet, rearing ….
[41] To assess participation in the project Mr Kother asked if the team members could
confirm whether or not they wanted to participate and stated that the project process would
begin on 5 March 2021.
[42] All the BAE team had wanted to participate, including Ms Chan. Whilst Mr Kother
and Ms Mathers would be overseeing the project, Mr Kother confirmed in the email that the
process would be driven by the participants.
[43] Mr Calero said that he had been on four weeks’ annual leave when the project started.
He returned to work on 9 March 2021 to find the project underway with eggs incubating and
the BAE team split into teams of two keepers caring for and monitoring three chicks each.
[44] Mr Calero said protocols for hand rearing, diet and all elements for caring for the birds
were to be researched and decided as a team. Once the eggs had hatched, the intention was to
join them in a group and for keepers to take turns caring for them overnight on a rostered basis
if they agreed to do so and their home environment was suitable.
[45] Prior to the first chick hatching Mr Calero said he sent an initial email on 17 March
2021, followed by a subsequent email after the first hatching on 18 March 2021 which set out
expectations and requirements of the project. Mr Calero also arranged two meetings for
feedback to be provided, the first of these was on 16 March 2021 at which the protocols were
decided.
[46] Ms Chan had been on annual leave and did not attend the first meeting on 16 March
2021 but confirmed she had received the email dated 18 March 2021 which had been the last

day of her leave. In the email Mr Calero gave specific details as to the diet weekly for the
chicks (keets), the temperature requirements, water and socialising.
[47] The email also set out that there would be a record sheet on which to record weights,
temperatures, food and time with them and their response. The email ended with an invitation
to contact either himself or Mr Kother if the team member had any concerns. In respect of the
temperature and record requirements the email stated:
TEMPERATURE
35 degrees 1st and 2nd week.. Then decrease by 2.5 degrees every week until room
temperature.
…
RECORD
There will be a record sheet to write weights, temperatures, food, and time with them
and their response. Feel free to add any information you consider would be helpful
in the future.
[48] Mr Calero said that Ms Chan had expressed concern about her understanding of the
protocols as she had returned from 13 days annual leave and had therefore not been involved
in the last stages of the project.
[49] Accordingly, he had met with Ms Chan and another BAE team member on 19 March
2021. They had not attended the meeting on 16 March 2021 so he updated them on the
protocols. Ms Chan confirmed at the investigation meeting that she had understood the
protocols.
[50] On 19 March 2021 Mr Calero sent an email to the BAE team including Ms Chan,
attaching ‘Keets sheet and information’ stating that the sheets were to be used to “write
everything about the keets. Starting from tomorrow. Every interaction with them, and
everything you consider important.”
[51] Mr Calero said some chicks had hatched on 19 March 2021 and he had taken these
chicks home to care for them overnight. Ms Chan had volunteered to be in charge of the BAE
team involved on the keet project the following day, Friday 20 March 2021, because Mr Calero
would be on a rostered day off as were Mr Kother and Ms Mathers. Mr Calero said he told Ms
Chan he would be available by telephone the following day if she wanted to contact him.
[52] Ms Chan said she had previously applied for and been interviewed for the 2IC role for
the BAE team. She had not been successful in that application, but she did want more
responsibility, so she asked to be the point of contact for the Guinea Fowl project on 20 March
2021.

Incident on Friday 20 March 2021
[53] The following morning Ms Chan transported the chicks in the incubator back to the
Zoo. The incubator was unplugged for transport and needed to be plugged in on arrival.
[54] Mr Kother said Ms Chan emailed him at 8.03 a.m. to inform him that she had arrived
at the Zoo with the chicks. He said the chicks were to be checked every hour as he and Mr
Calero had instructed.
[55] At approximately 11.00 o’clock a Guinea Fowl chick was found by another keeper to
be dead, and other chicks were in a distressed condition. The temperature in the incubator was
at 48℃, when it was meant to be at 35℃. Mr Kother said Ms Chan had telephoned him and
told him what had happened, and he asked her to complete an incident form.
[56] Ms Chan completed an incident form and emailed Mr Kother stating:
1 guinea fowl chick found deceased in incubator. Incubator thermostat had been
knocked and so incubator was at 50℃. The 5 other chicks were removed and given
water.
[57] Ms Chan also emailed Mr Kother stating:
I brought the incubator in at 7.30 and plugged it into the wall and flicked it on.
8.15 Egg 11 had hatched overnight and so we moved the processed egg 11 chick and
the one that hatched just before we left last night. We also pulled out the older chicks
for interactions.
9.30 I checked on the babies but didn’t pull them out cos they were asleep.
11.15 Tarrant checked the incubator while I was printing the record sheet and saw it
was at 50. The dead one was under the monkey. 2 were close to the door and the
others were all on the edges of the towel roll. He said they were doing a drinking
response.
[58] Mr Kother reported the incident to Ms Mathers and sent an email to the BAE
team involved on the keet project stating:
Unfortunately we have lost a guinea fowl keet due to keeper error. … It is my
understanding that the temperature dial on the brooder was knocked during transit and
has resulted in one bird passing away and the others being over-heated. … Please take
extra care during transit and make sure they are being checked regularly (once an hour
as agreed is fine) during the day to monitor the birds and check temperature.
[59] Mr Kother having discussed the incident with Ms Mathers, messaged Ms Chan advising
her that she would need to have supervised involvement with the project due to it being a serious
welfare issue until either he or Ms Mathers had spoken to her in person the following week.
[60] Mr Kother returned to work on 22 March 2021 and spoke to Mr Calero about the
condition of the chicks over the weekend. Mr Calero said Ms Chan had told him on the evening

of 20 March 2021 that the incubator had been off until at the first team check of the morning at
approximately 8.30 a.m.
[61] Mr Kother said this concerned him because Ms Chan had told him she had plugged the
incubator in at 7.30 a.m.
[62] Mr Kother said he held a discussion with the BAE team to get their account of what
had occurred and asked them specifically whether or not they recalled if the incubator was on
or running. After taking initial statements from the team, he spoke with Ms Mathers and
discussed interviewing the BAE team again and disclosing what Mr Calero said Ms Chan had
told him.
[63] At that stage it was established that the fact that the incubator had not been plugged in
had been omitted from accounts of events.
Meeting 25 March 2021
[64] On 25 March 2026 Mr Kother met with Ms Chan to give her an opportunity to clarify
what she had stated in the email to him on 20 March 2021 about the incubator having been
switched on. Ms Chan was accompanied by Mr Peterson. Mr Kother started the meeting by
telling her it was not a disciplinary meeting. The meeting was recorded.
[65] Mr Kother told Ms Chan that having spoken to Ms Ellis, Mr Tarrant and one other BAE
team member, their accounts of what had occurred differed from what she had stated in her
email to him on 20 March 2021.
[66] Ms Chan confirmed that she had carried out a check on the keets at 9.30 a,m, and agreed
that she had been the last to check them before they were discovered dead and/or distressed,
but that stated that “it wasn’t necessarily just me, and so I felt like I was being unfairly treated”
[67] Ms Chan said that there had been a few things she had missed, this was because she
had forgotten what had occurred. Mr Kother asked why, after she recalled that the incubator
had not been plugged in, she had not told him that was the case.
[68] Ms Chan’s response was that Ms Ellis told her she had already told him. Mr Kother
then asked if the first time she remembered had been the previous day (24 March) or the day
before that (23 March) to which Ms Chan responded yes.
[69] Mr Kother said Ms Chan told him she had decided which BAE team members would
be responsible for the chick checks throughout the day and had put herself down as being

responsible for doing the 9.30 a.m. check of the chicks, however she had not conducted a
temperature check at that time.
[70] He said he considered that the failure to properly set up the incubator was vital
information that should have been disclosed at the start of the process because it was important
in ensuring the well-being of the chicks. The importance of the temperature checks had been
stressed to the team members, and as an experienced zookeeper, Ms Chan should have been
aware of the importance of the checks.
[71] Ms Mathers said that Mr Kother emailed her a document with all the versions of events
for 20 March 2021 which each BAE team member involved in the Guinea Fowl project had
provided to him. Given the inconsistences in the statements, she decided to hold a meeting
with them. Ms Mathers said she invited Ms Nicholls the other Curator to also attend as neutral
third party.
Meeting with the Curators 29 March 2021
[72] Ms Mathers said during the meeting all the BAE team members present at the incident
on 20 March 2021 were provided with a copy of events and asked to confirm or deny them.
During the meeting amendments were made to the events and recorded. Ms Morgan-Fish was
interviewed separately as she had not been available on the day of the meeting, and her
comments were incorporated into the final version of events.
[73] The relevant team members received a copy of the finalised version of events and were
given the opportunity to add further comment but Ms Mathers said no further comments had
been received.
[74] Ms Mathers said she and Mr Grant consulted with the Zoo Director and the HR team
on the appropriate next steps. In Ms Chan’s case the next step was a disciplinary meeting.
Disciplinary Process April 2021
[75] On 19 April 2021 Mr Kother wrote to Ms Chan inviting her to attend a disciplinary
meeting on 27 April 2021. The letter stated:
On Saturday 20th of March there was an incident involving a death of a Guinea Fowl
chick and the near death of 6 others in the incubation room.
This prompted me to undertake an investigation. During my investigation into this
incident, which included talking to those involved as a group and individually, I found
discrepancies in the events that day, such as: who was present, when the brooder was
running and when it was not, who discovered the issue and who remedied it. I also
found there was a lack of accountability and learning from yourself, this was
demonstrated by the behaviour during and immediately following the incident. It was
disappointing that you were not forthcoming with important information even when
asked directly.

Geneva, this is not the first time you have been found to be dishonest and involved in
an incident that has resulted in the death of an animal. I am now writing to request
that you attend a disciplinary meeting as I allege that you have failed to perform the
duties of your role and have mislead me during the investigation into this matter. If
the allegations are confirmed there is a possibility that the following clauses in the
code of conduct may have been breached.
[76] The clauses were set as out as being
A. Misconduct
– Performance of Duties
- Failure to perform duties through careless, lazy or negligent behaviour
- Repeated failure to perform work to the required standard
- Failure to demonstrate Council behaviours to the required level
B. Serious misconduct : Disclosure: Dishonesty or misleading council.
[77] The misconduct and serious misconduct were demonstrated in that Ms Chan failed to:
a) set up the incubator correctly in accordance with the protocol on the morning of
20 March 2021;
b) assign team members to the hourly checks as required throughout the morning;
c) check the temperature of the incubator when she checked the keets on her own
volition at 9.30 a.m.;
d) report the incident through the required CIMS structure on the day, instead calling
Mr Kother who was on a rostered day off which resulted in the five remaining
chicks not being checked by a veterinarian until 22 March 2021;
e) despite being given five opportunities to give a truthful account about the incident.
In addition to amending her own version of accounts during the meeting on 25
March 2021 with Mr Kother, her version of events was in direct conflict with what
she had told Mr Calero.
[78] Mr Kother stated that Mr Mathers and Ms Clark, HR business Partner, would also be
present at the meeting, and she was entitled to have a support person or representative at the
meeting. Ms Chan was also told the meeting would be recorded and she would be provided
with a copy of the transcript.
[79] Ms Chan was notified that the disciplinary meeting was to take place on 27 April 2021.
Disciplinary meeting 27 April 2021
[80] Prior to the meeting Ms Chan had been medically certified as unable to attend for work
between 19 April to 3 May 2021. Ms Clark said she had been away on leave signed off 3 May
2021. On 27 April she was attending a pre-meeting with Ms Mathers and Mr Kother when she
realised Ms Chan’s medical certificate was still in place. She called Ms Chan to discuss this,
and Ms Chan arranged for an amended medical certificate which would permit her to attend the
disciplinary meeting.
[81] Ms Chan attended the disciplinary meeting accompanied by her parents. The meeting
was recorded and transcribed. Ms Chan confirmed during the Investigation Meeting that the
transcript was mostly accurate.

[82] During the meeting on Ms Chan stated that she:
• had failed to mention the incubator had been unplugged because she had
forgotten;
• did not check the temperature on the incubator each hour as set out in the
protocols
• did not check the temperature of the incubator at 9.30 a.m. when she checked
the chicks;
• considered she should not be singled out for the incident purely on the basis
that she was the point of contact that day; and
• she had relied on other people in the BAE team to help her with the incubator
• that if HCC was not happy with her work, she should not have been allowed to
take the chicks home; and
• the allegations of dishonesty should not include the incidents with the frog and
the parrot.
[83] During the meeting Ms Chan confirmed that she had lied during the incident with Ms
Morgan-Fish because she wanted to protect her, but that she had subsequently told Mr Kother
the truth afterwards.
[84] Ms Chan said she did not recall telling Mr Calero she had not plugged the incubator in
when she arrived at the Zoo, and said she explained that because the bird had not died as a result
of the brooder not having been plugged in, it was not an important detail. Afterwards she had
not mentioned it because Ms Ellis had mentioned it and therefore she did not think it necessary
to do so.
[85] There was an adjournment during the meeting. When it resumed Ms Clark advised Ms
Chan that what had been discussed during the meeting would be considered by the management
team and she would be advised of their view after they had done so.
[86] In relation to the dishonesty allegation, it was clarified that the prior incidents with the
frog and the parrot had been given as examples of where Ms Chan had been involved in animal
deaths previously. As a result HCC was concerned that there was a pattern of previous
behaviour when she was not performing work to the required standard, but the incident of
dishonesty related to the keets incident.
[87] On 29 April 2021 Ms Mathers wrote to Ms Chan outlining HCC’s preliminary findings
that she had:
i. Failed to perform the duties of your role through careless, lazy or negligent behaviour:

On 20 March you were responsible for the Guinea Fowl chicks, the set up and the
monitoring of the brooder they were contained in. I am confident that you knew how
to operate the brooder and the requirement to check the temperatures.
ii. Repeatedly failed to perform work to the required standard which has resulted in the
death of an animal:
…. This is not the first time your Team Leader had spoken to your about your
performance of duties in relation to the death of an animal. Whilst these matters did
not result in disciplinary action at that time, they were discussed with you at length
with expectations around your ongoing performance clarified.
iii. Failed to demonstrate behaviours to the level required of HCC employees:
Your behaviour throughout the investigation and in the disciplinary meeting are
inconsistent and incompatible with the level of behaviour required of HCC employees.
You mislead your Team Leader throughout the investigation by providing inaccurate
accounts of the incident and your involvement in it. You have shown no accountability
or responsibility for your actions that day. During the disciplinary meeting you took
every opportunity to place accountability and responsibility on others, … You have
not shown any remorse or concern for the animal’s death or the wellbeing of the chicks
who survived.
iv. Acted in a manner that was dishonest and misleading:
You mislead your team leader throughout the investigation by providing inaccurate
accounts of the incident and your involvement in it. This continued in the disciplinary
meeting. This is further supported by Mr Caler’s statement that you had known about
a problem with the brooder and that it had been off since 7am that morning … At
8.15am – 8.30 am this was discovered, and the brooder turned on. You then failed to
carry out the hourly checks required which resulted in the death of the chick from heat
exposure.
[88] Ms Mathers stated in conclusion:
Therefore, it is my preliminary finding that on balance you have acted in a a manner that
was dishonest and misleading. This action has eroded the trust and confidence that
underpins the employment relationship.
[89] The letter concluded by asking Ms Chan to provide her feedback on the preliminary
decision by 4 May 2021.
[90] Ms Chan responded to the preliminary findings on 6 May 2021 She stated that she had
been shocked at the preliminary outcome. She also stated that she did not have previous
experience in incubation or hand-rearing chicks, she had been on leave when the BAE team
briefing took place.
[91] Ms Chan stated that it had not been her intention to place blame on the other BAE team
members but had only intended to emphasise that she was not the only person involved with
the Guinea Fowl chicks.
[92] She stated she had been very distressed at the deaths of the Princess Parrot and
Hochsetter frog.

[111] I find HCC was entitled to conclude that Ms Chan understood how to operate the
incubator. There is no evidence that Ms Chan told HCC she did not understand how to use it
and ask for instruction in how to do so, which I would have expected since she volunteered to
be included in the keets project, and this would have been a fundamental piece of required
knowledge.
[112] In regard to checking the temperature, I find Ms Chan would have been aware of the
requirement to check the temperature of the chicks, this was set out in the email from Mr Calero
dated 18 March 2026. I find that ensuring the keets were kept at the optimum temperature to
thrive and that this was checked regularly would not be an unreasonable expectation of an
experienced zookeeper who had requested to be the person in charge for that day.
[113] Ms Chan acknowledged that she had not checked the temperature of the incubator when
setting it up, and I also observe that Ms Chan had volunteered to and did carry out a check on
the chicks at 9.30 a.m. but failed to check the temperature at that time.
[114] HCC considered Ms Chan had been dishonest in her accounts of the incident. During
the process conducted by HCC, Ms Chan made differing statements regarding the incident. On
20 March 2021 Ms Chan informed Mr Kother that the incubator had been switched on and the
temperature dial had been knocked.
[115] After Mr Kother heard from Mr Calero that Ms Chan had told him that the incubator
had not been plugged in and he raised this with the relevant BAE team members, they confirmed
that was the case. However Ms Chan did not alter her version of events until she was
specifically asked about it during the meeting held on 25 March 2021 when she confirmed that
the incubator had not been switched on at the start of the day as she had recorded on 20 March
2021.
[116] When asked why she had not told Mr Kother that earlier, her response was that it was
unnecessary for her to do so since another team member had already informed him of that.
[117] In light of the previous incident involving Ms Morgan-Fish a few weeks earlier when
Ms Chan had not been honest with Mr Kother, HCC considered she been circumspect with the
truth a further time despite having had the opportunity to alter her initial report in the days
between 20 and 25 March 2021.
[118] While no formal action had resulted from the two previous animal deaths in which Ms
Chan was involved, the evidence was that she had had discussions with Ms Mathers and Mr
Kother respectively about their expectations of her following each incident.

[125] In the letter dated 19 April 2021 Ms Chan was fully informed of the concerns HCC
wanted her to respond to and was provided her with a reasonable opportunity to do so.
[126] Ms Chan was also invited to have a support person or representative at the meeting
which was held on 27 April 2021, and she had the support of her parents at that meeting.
[127] Mr Kother, Ms Mathers and Ms Clark attended the meeting which was lengthy and
during which ms Chan had a full opportunity to respond to HCC’s concerns.
[128] Following the meeting a preliminary decision was issued, and Ms Chan was able to
provide feedback. It was only after Ms Chan provided her feedback and this was considered
that the final decision was made.
[129] It is submitted for Ms Chan that the disciplinary process was conducted without
procedural safeguards. I observe that before proceeding to invite Ms Chan to a disciplinary
meeting, there was consultation by Mr Kother and Ms Mathers with the Zoo Director and the
HR team, and that an HR Business Partner attended the disciplinary meeting on 27 April 2021.
[130] I find that HCC carried out a fair process.
[131] I determine that Ms Chan was justifiably dismissed by HCC.
Was Ms Chan unjustifiably disadvantaged by HCC’s handling of her bullying complaint?
[132] HCC has an Harassment, Bullying and Discrimination Policy. which set out the
procedure for raising bullying complaints. It was not necessary for Ms Chan to raise a bullying
complaint about her direct managers with them because in line with the policy, she could raise
her concern with any other member of the management team.
[133] During the investigation Ms Chan’s evidence was that she did not raise a formal
complaint of bullying. She had not raised any issues of concern about her managers with any
other members of the management team including the HR team, although she confirmed during
the Investigation Meeting that she knew she could do so.
[134] Mr Peterson’s evidence was that he had spoken to other members of the management
team when he had concerns and he was listened to when he did so.
[135] An employee can only be expected to respond to issues of which it is aware. In this
case it was not aware that Ms Chan had concerns that she felt subjected to bullying because she
did not raise those concerns.
